caption:
Federal prosecutors say three men used AI to fake the voices and faces of CEOs on calls with accounting staff.
The calls came with fake lawyers and "secret deals," and at least $129 million was wired away.
Victims include two hospital systems, a bank and a pet food company.

Would you catch a fake call from your own boss?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: Gizmodo, SOFX · Photo: Bluestonex / Unsplash
threads_text: Prosecutors say three men used AI clones of CEOs and lawyers on phone and video calls to get staff to wire out at least $129 million. Hospitals and a bank were among the victims. Would you trust a video call from your boss asking for a secret wire?

paragraphs.text: Federal prosecutors in the Southern District of New York unsealed an indictment on November 5, 2026, charging three men with running a fraud scheme that used artificial intelligence to impersonate company executives and lawyers. According to the indictment, at least $129 million was stolen from businesses that included hospital systems, a bank and a mutual fund company.

The defendants are Jacob Soall, 41, of Marbella, Spain, and the United Kingdom; Sharon Hazan, 54, of Israel; and Guy Sheetrit, 42, of Israel and the United Arab Emirates. Each faces seven counts, including conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud, aggravated identity theft and money laundering. All three are presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

Prosecutors say the conspiracy ran from about July 2024 to about February 2026 and targeted thousands of companies around the world. The usual targets were accounting employees who had authority to approve large wire transfers. The group allegedly used AI to mimic an executive's voice, and in some cases the executive's appearance, on phone or video calls.

According to Gizmodo's account of the indictment, a typical attempt began with an email that appeared to come from the company's chief executive, sent through an electronic signature service, asking for help with a confidential deal and attaching a nondisclosure agreement. A call with a supposed attorney followed. That person often used the identity of a real lawyer at the European office of a large law firm, described a secret transaction such as an acquisition and supplied the wire instructions.

Soall mostly posed as British attorneys, prosecutors say, and used a handwritten script titled "Lawyer Call" that stressed confidentiality and insider trading concerns so employees would not discuss the transfer with colleagues. Hazan and Sheetrit allegedly handled the laundering. SOFX reported that the money moved through accounts in nine countries, including the United States, Spain and China, before it was converted to cryptocurrency and divided.
The victims named in the indictment

The indictment does not name the companies but describes them. A Missouri hospital system lost about $4.83 million in November 2024, a Rhode Island bank about $2.68 million that same month and a California hospital system about $2.97 million in December 2024. A UK financial technology company lost about $11.58 million in March 2025, a Massachusetts mutual fund company about $4.64 million in April 2025 and a Florida pet food company about $5.24 million in June 2025. An attempt against a major New York investment bank in October 2024 failed when its back office stopped a wire of about $2.85 million.

Soall was arrested in Spain in June, Hazan in Spain in August and Sheetrit in the United Kingdom in September, and U.S. extradition requests for all three are pending. Prosecutors say Hazan, who was convicted of conspiracy to commit bank fraud in the same court in 2008, boasted of laundering more than $400 million over three years. SOFX put the combined maximum sentence at 104 years; any sentence would be set by a judge after a conviction.

According to SOFX, the alleged total is about five times the $25.6 million that the engineering firm Arup lost to a deepfake scam in 2024, and far above the roughly $30 million in AI-linked business email compromise losses reported to the FBI for 2025.

The case shows how voice and video cloning fit into an older crime. Business email compromise has long relied on fake urgency and secrecy. A convincing voice on the phone removes one of the checks employees were trained to use, which is calling the executive to confirm.
The next step is extradition. Whether the three men are brought to New York will decide when the evidence, including how the AI tools were used, is tested in court.
